place.zh: 石坳村 · 屋后柴垛 · 半夜

_weather: 「柴垛上没人，只有月亮」: a moonlit night (Hanli 2026-10-14: 「可以，月夜标成晴」)

setup.zh: 日头偏西，你去村东头背回那只缸，吴婆婆讲了一个很短的故事：一口鼎，一条龙，一张掉下来的弓——鼎湖，乌号。半夜里，柴垛上，它睁开了一只眼睛。你问她：真的有仙人？
setup.en: Toward evening you fetch the crock back from the east end, and Granny Wu tells a very short story: a *ding*, a dragon, a bow that fell — Dinghu, Wuhao. At midnight on the woodpile it opens one eye. You ask her: are there really immortals?

recap.zh: 吴婆婆讲了鼎湖：上去的上去了，留下的，就守着一张弓。银月醒了一回：仙人是真的，凡人能修。次夜她留下洗髓丹、《吐纳经》和一个「藏」字，钻进了木牌；那声谢谢，她没听见。
recap.en: Granny Wu told of Dinghu: those who went up went up; those left behind kept a bow. Yinyue woke once: immortals are real, mortals can cultivate. The next night she left a Marrow-Washing Pill, *The Classic of Breathing* and one word — hide — and went into the token; the thank-you, she never heard.

zh: 柴垛上，一团凉冰冰的银毛。
断口渗出的血，是银的，像落了一层霜。
半夜，它睁开了一只眼睛。
en: On the woodpile, a cold curl of silver fur.
The blood from its cuts is silver, like a fall of frost.
At midnight, it opens one eye.

story.zh:
吴婆婆的脸已经朝着西边了，听见缸响，道：「弓，回来了？」她便仰着脸，讲了一个很短的故事。

早年间，天底下头一个皇帝，在一座山底下铸了一口鼎。鼎成那天，天上下来一条龙接他。剩下一个小官儿挤不上去，扑上去抓住了龙须；龙须扯断了，跟着掉下来的，还有那皇帝的一张弓。后来的人，管那地方叫鼎湖，管那张弓，叫乌号。

小满问道：「那张弓，后来有人拉开过吗？」吴婆婆慢慢地露出一个笑来：「你问得好。」只自言自语地添了一句：「修仙修仙，修成个想上天的人，也就修到头了。」

那天夜里，小满把「围脖」抱到了屋后的柴垛上。半夜里，它睁开了一只眼睛，头一句便是：「……吵死了。你喘气那么大声干什么。」有一个问题，他憋了一整天：「我爹说那是编的。仙人，真有？」

「你爹说错了。」银月道，「仙人，是真的。」「他们从前也都是凡人，跟你一样，饿了就啃饼。后来学会了把天地间的灵气，一点一点收进自己的身子里，像你娘往缸里存米。」

小满才问：「骑龙的……是像吴婆婆讲的那个皇帝那样？」银月的耳朵，动了一下。她看着月亮，看了很久，才道：「……本王不记得了。」她说的是「不记得」，不是「不知道」。

「那……我也能？」「能。但很难。一百个，九十九个老死了事。」她睡着了，尾巴尖儿搭在他手腕上，搭在他娘打的那个方方正正的结上。
story.en:
Granny Wu's face was already turned to the west. Hearing the crock rattle, she said, "The bow — it's come back?" Then she lifted her face and told a very short story.

In the old days, the very first emperor under heaven cast a cauldron at the foot of a mountain. On the day the cauldron was finished, a dragon came down from the sky to fetch him. One minor official was left who couldn't squeeze on; he threw himself at the dragon's whiskers, caught hold. The whiskers snapped, and along with them fell the emperor's bow. People after that called the place Cauldron Lake, and called the bow Crow's Cry.

Xiaoman asked, "That bow — did anyone ever draw it after?" Granny Wu slowly let a smile come. "That's a good question." She only added, to herself: "Cultivate, cultivate. Once you've cultivated yourself into someone who wants to go up to heaven, you've cultivated as far as you'll go."

That night Xiaoman carried the "scarf" up onto the woodpile behind the house. In the middle of the night it opened one eye, and the first thing it said was, "…What a racket. Why do you breathe so loud?" There was a question he'd been holding in all day. "Pa says that's made up. Immortals — are they real?"

"Your father's wrong," Yinyue said. "Immortals are real." "Every one of them was a mortal once, just like you; hungry, they gnawed flatbread. Later they learned to take the spirit qi of heaven and earth and store it in their own bodies, bit by bit, the way your mother stores rice in the crock."

Xiaoman asked, "And riding a dragon… is that like the emperor in Granny Wu's story?" Yinyue's ear twitched. She looked at the moon, looked at it so long, before she said, "…This queen doesn't remember." What she said was "doesn't remember", not "doesn't know".

"Then… could I do it too?" "You could. But it's hard. Out of a hundred, ninety-nine just die of old age and that's that." She was asleep, the tip of her tail lying across his wrist, across the square, neat knot his mother had tied.

story_full.zh:
日头偏西，他娘叫他去村东头把缸背回来。吴婆婆的脸已经朝着西边了，听见缸响，道：「弓，回来了？」小满道：「回来了。」她便仰着脸，讲了一个很短的故事。

早年间，天底下头一个皇帝，在一座山底下铸了一口鼎。鼎成那天，天上下来一条龙接他，皇帝骑上去，大官、娘娘跟着爬上去七十几个。剩下一个小官儿挤不上去，扑上去抓住了龙须，吊在半空里；他有个闺女，才七八岁，在底下仰着脸，一声一声地喊爹。龙须扯断了，人都掉了下来，跟着掉下来的，还有那皇帝的一张弓。后来的人，管那地方叫鼎湖，管那张弓，叫乌号。她讲到那闺女仰着脸喊爹，自己的脸也仰着，朝着天上。

小满道：「那闺女呢？」吴婆婆道：「……哭呗。」又道：「上去的上去了，留下的，就守着一张弓。」小满问道：「那张弓，后来有人拉开过吗？」吴婆婆转过脸来，朝着他，慢慢地露出一个笑来：「你问得好。」便不再往下说了，只自言自语地添了一句：「修仙修仙，修成个想上天的人，也就修到头了。」

那天夜里，小满把「围脖」抱到了屋后的柴垛上。柴垛上没人，只有月亮。

它一整天都没醒。身子还是凉的，尾根上那八道断口又渗出血来，银色的，一滴一滴落在柴草上，像下了一层霜。他把它捧在膝盖上，拿身子挡着风。半夜里，它睁开了一只眼睛，头一句便是：「……吵死了。你喘气那么大声干什么。」

小满长长地松了一口气，差点哭出来。有一个问题，他憋了一整天：「吴婆婆讲过，蒙山顶上住过一个骑白鹤的老头，活了八百岁。我爹说那是编的。仙人，真有？」

「你爹说错了。」银月道，「仙人，是真的。本王见过的仙人，比你见过的鸡还多。」她哼了一声，「他们从前也都是凡人，跟你一样，饿了就啃饼。后来学会了把天地间的灵气，一点一点收进自己的身子里，像你娘往缸里存米。存够了，不老，不病，力能搬山。——就这么点事，叫修仙。」

柴垛上很静。隔了好一会儿，小满才问：「骑龙的……是像吴婆婆讲的那个皇帝那样？」银月的耳朵，动了一下。她看着月亮，看了很久，久到小满以为她又睡着了，才道：「……本王不记得了。」她说的是「不记得」，不是「不知道」。小满当时没听出这两样有什么分别。

「那……我也能？」「能。但很难。一百个，九十九个老死了事。」「灵气是什么？经脉是什么？」「问他们。这世上有一群人，专门教人修仙。比本王有耐心。……当然，没本王教得好。」她的声音越来越轻，轻到后来，便没有了。她睡着了，尾巴尖儿搭在他手腕上，搭在他娘打的那个方方正正的结上。
story_full.en:
When the sun was sinking west, his mother sent him to the east end of the village to bring the crock back. Granny Wu's face was already turned to the west. Hearing the crock rattle, she said, "The bow — it's come back?" Xiaoman said, "It's come back." Then she lifted her face and told a very short story.

In the old days, the very first emperor under heaven cast a cauldron at the foot of a mountain. On the day the cauldron was finished, a dragon came down from the sky to fetch him. The emperor climbed on, and his great officials and his ladies climbed on after him, seventy-odd of them. One minor official was left who couldn't squeeze on; he threw himself at the dragon's whiskers, caught hold, and hung there in mid-air. He had a daughter, only seven or eight, down below with her face turned up, calling "Pa" over and over. The whiskers snapped, and the people fell down, and along with them fell the emperor's bow. People after that called the place Cauldron Lake, and called the bow Crow's Cry. When she got to the daughter with her face turned up calling for her father, her own face was turned up too, towards the sky.

Xiaoman said, "And the daughter?" Granny Wu said, "…Cried, what else?" Then: "The ones who went up went up. The one left behind kept a bow." Xiaoman asked, "That bow — did anyone ever draw it after?" Granny Wu turned her face towards him and slowly let a smile come. "That's a good question." And she said no more, only added, to herself: "Cultivate, cultivate. Once you've cultivated yourself into someone who wants to go up to heaven, you've cultivated as far as you'll go."

That night Xiaoman carried the "scarf" up onto the woodpile behind the house. There was nobody on the woodpile, only the moon.

It hadn't woken all day. Its body was still cold, and the eight stumps at the root of its tail had started oozing blood again, silver, dropping one drop at a time onto the brushwood, like a layer of frost. He held it on his knees and shielded it from the wind with his body. In the middle of the night it opened one eye, and the first thing it said was, "…What a racket. Why do you breathe so loud?"

Xiaoman let out a long breath and nearly cried. There was a question he'd been holding in all day. "Granny Wu said an old man who rode a white crane once lived on top of Mount Meng and lived to eight hundred. Pa says that's made up. Immortals — are they real?"

"Your father's wrong," Yinyue said. "Immortals are real. This queen has seen more immortals than you've seen chickens." She snorted. "Every one of them was a mortal once, just like you; hungry, they gnawed flatbread. Later they learned to take the spirit qi of heaven and earth and store it in their own bodies, bit by bit, the way your mother stores rice in the crock. Store enough and you don't age, don't sicken, and you're strong enough to move a mountain. — That's all there is to it. It's called cultivating immortality."

It was very quiet on the woodpile. After a good while Xiaoman asked, "And riding a dragon… is that like the emperor in Granny Wu's story?" Yinyue's ear twitched. She looked at the moon, looked at it so long Xiaoman thought she'd gone back to sleep, before she said, "…This queen doesn't remember." What she said was "doesn't remember", not "doesn't know". At the time Xiaoman didn't hear any difference between the two.

"Then… could I do it too?" "You could. But it's hard. Out of a hundred, ninety-nine just die of old age and that's that." "What's spirit qi? What are meridians?" "Ask them. There's a whole crowd of people in this world whose job is teaching people to cultivate. More patient than this queen. …Not as good at teaching as this queen, of course." Her voice got softer and softer, until it wasn't there at all. She was asleep, the tip of her tail lying across his wrist, across the square, neat knot his mother had tied.

story.zh:
到了夜里，是银月把他叫醒的。她的样子，比昨天更差了。整个身子薄得像一层纸，月光能从她身上透将过去。她道：「听着。本王要睡一阵子。」「多久？」「不知道。伤太重，得闭关。」「在本王醒过来之前，你得自己走。」

她从颈子底下一只旧得发黑的小布袋里，一样一样往外吐东西。头一样是一颗药丸。她道：「洗髓丹。今夜就泡。疼也别喊出声。」

第二样是一卷竹简。她道：「《吐纳经》。最粗浅的入门功夫，仙界三岁的狐狸崽子都会。看不懂，也要背。」然后她看着他，一个字一个字地说道：「**藏。**」

「藏本王，藏你自己。」她道，「在你打得过所有人之前，不许让任何人知道本王，不许让任何人知道你在修炼。」「我娘也不能说？」银月道：「你娘，用不着你说。」「那什么时候能不藏？」「等你把欺负过你的人，一个一个，都踩在脚底下的时候。」

「还有……本王在找一个地方……一个名字……」「……想不起来了。等你……听见了，本王会知道的……」她的身子在月光里一点一点地淡下去。

他张开嘴。「银月——」她看着他。只剩一双金色的眼睛，还在月光里亮着，等着他往下说。可不知怎的，话一出口，却变成了：「……你还欠我一张饼呢。」

她的身子化成了一缕银光，钻进了吴婆婆给他的那块狐纹木牌。木牌上那只蜷着的小狐狸，九条尾巴里，有一条亮了，银的，一明，一暗。他又道：「你还欠我一张饼呢。」木牌，暖了一下。

他把木牌捧起来，凑到嘴边，很小很小声地说道：「银月。」停了一停。「谢谢。」木牌凉凉的，没有暖。它睡得太沉了，听不见。
story.en:
That night it was Yinyue who woke him. She looked worse than yesterday. Her whole body was as thin as a sheet of paper, and the moonlight shone right through her. She said, "Listen. This queen has to sleep for a while." "How long?" "Don't know. The wounds are too deep. I have to go into seclusion." "Until this queen wakes up, you have to go on by yourself."

From a little cloth bag under her neck, so old it had gone black, she spat things out one by one. The first was a pill. She said, "Marrow-Washing Pill. Soak in it tonight. However much it hurts, don't cry out."

The second was a roll of bamboo slips. She said, "*The Scroll of Breath*. The crudest beginner's practice; every three-year-old fox cub in the immortal realm knows it. Even if you can't understand it, learn it by heart." Then she looked at him and said, one word at a time: "**Hide.**"

"Hide this queen, and hide yourself," she said. "Until you can beat everyone, nobody is allowed to know about this queen, and nobody is allowed to know you're cultivating." "Can't I even tell my ma?" Yinyue said, "Your ma doesn't need you to tell her." "Then when can I stop hiding?" "When you've put everyone who ever bullied you under your feet, one by one."

"One more thing… this queen is looking for a place… a name…" "…Can't remember. When you… hear it, this queen will know…" Her body was fading in the moonlight bit by bit.

He opened his mouth. "Yinyue—" She looked at him. Only a pair of golden eyes still shone in the moonlight, waiting for him to go on. But somehow, when it came out, it turned into: "…You still owe me a flatbread, you know."

Her body turned into a thread of silver light, and slipped into the fox-carved wooden tablet Granny Wu had given him. On the tablet, of the little curled-up fox's nine tails, one lit up, silver, glowing, dimming. He said again, "You still owe me a flatbread, you know." The tablet grew warm, for a moment.

He lifted the tablet up to his lips and said, very, very quietly, "Yinyue." He paused. "Thank you." The tablet stayed cool. She was sleeping too deeply. She couldn't hear.

story_full.zh:
第二天，她没有醒。小满隔一会儿便低头看一眼胸口，他娘问他胸口疼？他说不疼，看看还在不在。

到了夜里，是银月把他叫醒的。小满睡在柴垛上——他跟他娘说屋里挤，他娘看了他一眼，给了他一床破棉絮——睡到半夜，只觉得胸口一凉，像揣着的一块冰忽然化开了。他一激灵坐了起来，那团银毛已经从他怀里钻了出来，蹲在柴垛顶上，对着月亮。

她的样子，比昨天更差了。银色的血是不渗了，可整个身子薄得像一层纸，月光能从她身上透将过去。薄一分，又薄一分——她在谷里说的，原来是这个样子。她道：「听着。本王要睡一阵子。」「多久？」「不知道。伤太重，得闭关。」她看着他，「在本王醒过来之前，你得自己走。」

她从颈子底下一只旧得发黑的小布袋里，一样一样往外吐东西。头一样是一颗药丸，黑乎乎的，鸽子蛋那么大，像烂菜叶子泡了三天的味儿。她道：「洗髓丹。今夜就泡。疼也别喊出声。」小满捏着鼻子道：「洗……洗什么？」「洗你那一身脉。」她喘了一口气，像背一句背了几千年的老话：「凡人有此八脉，俱属阴神，闭而不开。」小满道：「八脉是什么？」「你身子里八条水渠，都堵着。」「那堵着的，怎么开？」她没有答，眼皮往下一垂，接着往外吐。

第二样是一卷竹简，绳子都快烂了，竹片上还有虫蛀的眼儿。可它一落在柴草上，四下里的夜气便清了一清，像下过一场小雨；小满拿在手里，竹片竟是温的。她道：「《吐纳经》。最粗浅的入门功夫，仙界三岁的狐狸崽子都会。看不懂，也要背。」然后她看着他，一个字一个字地说道：「**藏。**」小满道：「藏什么？」

「藏本王，藏你自己。」她道，「在你打得过所有人之前，不许让任何人知道本王，不许让任何人知道你在修炼。能装傻就装傻，能示弱就示弱。——你那个吃饼的鬼，就很好。往后，你就是那个见了鬼吓得打摆子的傻孩子。」「我娘也不能说？」银月道：「你娘，用不着你说。」

小满想起他娘理围脖的那只手，想起她那句「这条围脖，挺暖和的吧」，便不再问了。「那什么时候能不藏？」「等你把欺负过你的人，一个一个，都踩在脚底下的时候。」

她的眼皮越来越沉，声音也越来越低：「还有……本王在找一个地方……一个名字……」她皱着眉，很用力地想，「……想不起来了。等你……听见了，本王会知道的……」小满道：「什么地方？什么名字？你说个大概，我替你留心——」她却已经不说了。她的身子在月光里一点一点地淡下去，淡得像灶膛里最后那一缕青烟。

小满急了。这一回，她是真的要走了，要到一个他够不着的地方去。那个字，这时候再不说，便真的来不及了。他张开嘴。「银月——」她看着他。她已经淡得快看不见了，只剩一双金色的眼睛，还在月光里亮着，等着他往下说。

他张着嘴，那个字就在舌头尖上。可不知怎的，话一出口，却变成了：「……你还欠我一张饼呢。」那双金色的眼睛，眨了一下。她的身子化成了一缕银光。那缕光绕着他转了一圈，轻轻擦过他的脸，凉凉的，钻进了他怀里，钻进了吴婆婆给他的那块狐纹木牌。木牌上那只蜷着的小狐狸，九条尾巴里，有一条亮了，银的，一明，一暗，像在很慢、很慢地呼吸。小满低头看着那块木牌，小声道：「……喂，你还在吗？」木牌没有回答。他又道：「你还欠我一张饼呢。」木牌，暖了一下。

他在柴垛上坐了很久，把木牌捧起来，凑到嘴边，很小很小声地说道：「银月。」停了一停。

「谢谢。」

木牌凉凉的，没有暖。那条银色的尾巴，照旧一明，一暗。它睡得太沉了，听不见。
story_full.en:
The next day she didn't wake. Every little while Xiaoman looked down at his chest. His mother asked if his chest hurt. He said no, he was just checking it was still there.

That night it was Yinyue who woke him. Xiaoman slept on the woodpile — he'd told his mother it was crowded in the house, and his mother had given him a look and then given him a ragged old quilt — and in the middle of the night his chest suddenly felt cold, as if a lump of ice he was carrying had melted all at once. He sat bolt upright. The ball of silver fur had already crept out of his jacket and was crouched on top of the woodpile, facing the moon.

She looked worse than yesterday. The silver blood had stopped seeping, but her whole body was as thin as a sheet of paper, and the moonlight shone right through her. Thinner, and thinner again — so this was what she'd meant in the valley. She said, "Listen. This queen has to sleep for a while." "How long?" "Don't know. The wounds are too deep. I have to go into seclusion." She looked at him. "Until this queen wakes up, you have to go on by yourself."

From a little cloth bag under her neck, so old it had gone black, she spat things out one by one. The first was a pill, dark and murky, as big as a pigeon's egg, smelling like rotten cabbage leaves soaked for three days. She said, "Marrow-Washing Pill. Soak in it tonight. However much it hurts, don't cry out." Xiaoman held his nose. "Wash… wash what?" "Wash all the channels in that body of yours." She drew a breath, like someone reciting a saying she'd recited for thousands of years: "Mortals have these eight channels; all belong to the yin spirit; they are shut and do not open." Xiaoman said, "What are the eight channels?" "Eight water channels in your body, and they're all blocked." "And blocked ones — how do you open them?" She didn't answer. Her eyelids drooped, and she went on spitting things out.

The second was a roll of bamboo slips. The cord was nearly rotted through, and the slips had wormholes in them. But the moment it landed on the brushwood the night air around them cleared, as if after a light rain, and when Xiaoman picked it up the slips were actually warm. She said, "*The Scroll of Breath*. The crudest beginner's practice; every three-year-old fox cub in the immortal realm knows it. Even if you can't understand it, learn it by heart." Then she looked at him and said, one word at a time: "**Hide.**" Xiaoman said, "Hide what?"

"Hide this queen, and hide yourself," she said. "Until you can beat everyone, nobody is allowed to know about this queen, and nobody is allowed to know you're cultivating. Play the fool wherever you can; look weak wherever you can. — That ghost of yours that eats flatbread was very good. From now on, you're the silly boy who saw a ghost and got the shakes." "Can't I even tell my ma?" Yinyue said, "Your ma doesn't need you to tell her."

Xiaoman remembered his mother's hand straightening the scarf, and her "That scarf's nice and warm, isn't it", and didn't ask any more. "Then when can I stop hiding?" "When you've put everyone who ever bullied you under your feet, one by one."

Her eyelids were getting heavier and heavier, and her voice lower and lower. "One more thing… this queen is looking for a place… a name…" She frowned, trying very hard to think. "…Can't remember. When you… hear it, this queen will know…" Xiaoman said, "What place? What name? Just tell me roughly, I'll keep an ear out for you—" But she had stopped talking. Her body was fading in the moonlight bit by bit, fading like the last wisp of blue smoke in the stove.

Xiaoman panicked. This time she really was going, going somewhere he couldn't reach. That word — if he didn't say it now, it would truly be too late. He opened his mouth. "Yinyue—" She looked at him. She'd faded so much she was nearly invisible; only a pair of golden eyes still shone in the moonlight, waiting for him to go on.

His mouth was open, and the word was on the tip of his tongue. But somehow, when it came out, it turned into: "…You still owe me a flatbread, you know." The golden eyes blinked once. Her body turned into a thread of silver light. The light circled him once, brushed his face lightly, cool, and slipped inside his jacket, into the fox-carved wooden tablet Granny Wu had given him. On the tablet, of the little curled-up fox's nine tails, one lit up, silver, glowing, dimming, as if breathing very, very slowly. Xiaoman looked down at the tablet and said quietly, "…Hey, are you still there?" The tablet didn't answer. He said again, "You still owe me a flatbread, you know." The tablet grew warm, for a moment.

He sat on the woodpile a long time, then lifted the tablet up to his lips and said, very, very quietly, "Yinyue." He paused.

"Thank you."

The tablet stayed cool. It didn't warm. The silver tail went on glowing and dimming as before. She was sleeping too deeply. She couldn't hear.
